Companies that are *structurally* downstream from BP (up‑to‑two tiers) | Tier | Company (sector) | Why it appears in the supply graph | |------|------------------|------------------------------------| | **Tier 1** | CPC Corp/Taiwan – petrochemical feedstock maker | Receives propylene/propylene from BP’s naphtha crackers. | | | Indian Oil (India) – refined fuels & lubricants | Refines and markets BP‑supplied crude and fuel streams. | | | Formosa Petrochemical (Taiwan) – aromatics (paraxylene, benzene) | Uses BP‑derived ethylene/propylene as feedstock. | | | LG Chem (South Korea) – petrochemicals & battery cathode materials | Sources olefins and other intermediates from BP’s Asian joint ventures. | |  | **Volkswagen** (Germany) – passenger & commercial vehicles | Listed by the graph as a downstream customer of BP‑derived fuels/lubricants. | |  | Guangdong Delian (China) – automotive fine chemicals (coolants, brake fluids, lubricants) | Uses BP‑produced petrochemical intermediates. | |  | Jordan Petroleum Refinery (Jordan) – refined petroleum products | Processes crude supplied by BP. | |  | POSCO (South Korea) – steel producer | Consumes BP‑derived coke/energy inputs. | |  | Grupo Pochteca (Mexico) – industrial chemical & raw‑material distribution | Distributes BP petrochemical outputs. | |  | Ternium (Luxembourg) – flat‑rolled steel | Uses BP‑produced energy and lubricants. | |  | Guangzhou Development (China) – electric power & integrated energy | Purchases BP natural‑gas/energy services. | | **Tier 2** (selected, high‑relevance examples) | Tata Motors (India), Stellantis (Netherlands), Kia (South Korea), Hyundai Motor (South Korea), Toyota Motor (Japan), Tesla (USA), BYD (China) – automotive OEMs that rely on fuels, lubricants or petrochemical feedstocks supplied by the Tier‑1 firms above. | | | Samsung Electronics (South Korea) – automotive electronics & semiconductors (uses BP‑derived chemicals in manufacturing). | | | Robert Bosch (Germany) – fuel‑injection and electronic control systems (uses BP lubricants/fuels). | | | SK Innovation (South Korea) – EV lithium‑ion battery cells (requires BP‑produced petrochemical precursors). | | | Glencore (UK) – cobalt mining (energy & fuel supplied by BP). | | | … *(the full Tier‑2 list contains >150 additional firms across steel, chemicals, automotive parts, utilities and transportation equipment; they are all reachable within two hops from BP.)* | > **Note:** The traversal tool only indicates *structural* connections – i.e., that a company is listed as a downstream customer or an alternative supplier in the underlying supply‑chain model. It does **not** itself confirm whether those customers were actually impacted by the April 2010 event. --- ### 2. Evidence gathered for the disruption | Company | Source(s) consulted | What the source says | |---------|--------------------|----------------------| | **BP (the disrupted firm)** | *search_corpus* – “BP disruption April 2010 supply” (10‑result query) – extracts from BP’s 2009/2010 annual filing (filed 03‑Mar‑2010). | • Describes BP’s petrochemical joint ventures in Malaysia and China, its naphtha crackers, refinery capacities, wind‑farm assets, and overall operating performance.
• No explicit mention of a supply interruption on 20 April 2010; the filing is a routine annual report covering the prior year. | | **Volkswagen** | *get_supplier_info* – attempted to retrieve Volkswagen’s own filing (no record found). | No filing available in the database, therefore no direct statement from VW about any BP‑related impact. | | **Other Tier 1/Tier 2 firms** | None (all remaining tool calls exhausted). | No company‑specific filings or corpus mentions were retrieved that explicitly link these downstream firms to a disruption at BP on the date in question. | The only concrete documentary evidence we have is BP’s own 2009‑10 filing, which outlines its production capacities and joint‑venture structures (e.g., Ethylene Malaysia Sdn Bhd., Polyethylene Malaysia Sdn Bhd., SECCO in China). Those sections demonstrate the *potential* pathways through which downstream customers could be affected if BP’s feedstock or fuel supply were interrupted. However, the filing does **not** describe any such interruption occurring on 20 April 2010. --- ### 3. What could not be confirmed | Company / Group | Reason for lack of confirmation | |-----------------|---------------------------------| | **Volkswagen** (and all other downstream OEMs listed) | No SEC‑type filing was found for Volkswagen; the corpus search returned only BP’s own text, which does not mention any impact on VW. Consequently we cannot verify whether VW experienced a supply shortfall or operational disruption linked to BP at that time. | | **Tier 2 automotive and steel firms** (e.g., Tata Motors, Stellantis, POSCO, Samsung Electronics, etc.) | No targeted filings or corpus hits were retrieved for these entities concerning the April 2010 event. Their inclusion in the graph is purely structural; we have no evidence they reported any disruption. | | **Chemical and energy utilities** (e.g., LG Chem, SK Innovation, Glencore) | Same as above – no direct statements or filings were accessed that confirm an impact. | | **Exact nature of the “disruption”** | The investigation was prompted by a report of a disruption at BP on 20 April 2010, but none of the documents examined (BP’s annual filing, the limited corpus queries) describe what the event was (e.g., plant outage, logistics issue, cyber‑incident). Without that detail we cannot assess the likely downstream consequences. | --- ### 4. Overall assessment * **Structural exposure:** A very large set of companies – spanning petrochemicals, fuels, automotive OEMs, steel producers, electronics manufacturers and utilities – are linked to BP within two tiers of the supply‑chain graph. In principle, any interruption at BP could ripple through these downstream firms. * **Documented impact:** The only publicly available evidence in this investigation is BP’s own 2009‑10 filing, which outlines its operations but does not mention a specific disruption on or around 20 April 2010. No downstream company’s filing or public statement was found that confirms they experienced any material effect from such an event. * **Confidence level:** Because the investigation exhausted the allowed four tool calls before obtaining direct confirmation for any downstream firm, the picture remains **incomplete**. We can state with confidence which companies are *potentially* at risk based on the supply‑chain model, but we cannot substantiate that any of them actually suffered a disruption as a result of the reported BP incident. --- ### 5. Next steps (if further resources become available) 1. **Targeted filing retrieval** for the most critical downstream firms (e.g., Volkswagen, Toyota, Tesla, POSCO, LG Chem) to see whether they disclosed supply‑chain impacts in their 2010 quarterly or annual reports. 2. **News‑media search** around the specific date (20 April 2010) for any press releases or news articles describing a BP outage, refinery incident, logistics strike, cyber‑attack, etc., and any quoted statements from downstream customers. 3. **Supply‑chain partner verification** – contact joint‑venture partners (e.g., SECCO, EMSB/PEMSB) for operational notices issued at that time. --- **Bottom line:** The supply‑graph shows a broad network of companies that could be affected by a BP disruption, but the limited documentary evidence retrieved in this investigation does not confirm any actual downstream impact on those firms as of 20 April 2010. The analysis is therefore **incomplete** and should be supplemented with additional filings or contemporaneous news sources to reach a definitive conclusion.
